title: Natural flood management benefits of catchment‐scale woodland creation in the UK uplands
content:
Increased woodland cover in an upland catchment reduces peak stream flow by more than 5% during large storm events.


Abstract

Woodlands typically reduce downstream flooding, but the magnitude of flood risk reduction at a catchment scale remains uncertain. Although flood mitigation is a common objective of woodland creation, land managers often lack catchment-specific information to guide effective woodland design. We collaborated with land managers to simulate the flood mitigation benefits of a proposed new woodland within a 10.9-km2 upland catchment in North Yorkshire, UK. Using Spatially Distributed TOPMODEL, combined with empirical soil and vegetation data, we assessed how different woodland creation scenarios would influence peak streamflow under a range of storm events. For a 1 in 10-year storm, we simulated a 2.6% reduction in peak streamflow for each 10-percentage point increase in catchment woodland cover. The proposed 1.6 km2 of new woodland, resulting in catchment scale woodland cover of 28.2%, reduced simulated peak streamflow for a 1 in 10-year storm event by 5.1% and for a 1 in 50-year storm event by 5.3%. We estimated the 100-year flood regulation service of the proposed woodland to be worth £2.02 ± 0.54 million, equivalent to £12,300 ± 3300 per hectare of woodland, comparable to the financial value of carbon sequestration of the woodland. Practical Implication Our study demonstrates the substantial potential of catchment-scale woodland creation for natural flood management in the UK uplands. It also highlights the benefits of quantifying the flood mitigation potential during the woodland design stage.
